gdpr.label: Article 5(1)(a)
gdpr.title: Principles relating to processing of personal data

gdpr.label: Article 6(1) to (3)
gdpr.title: Lawfulness of processing

rows.obligation: Process personal data lawfully, fairly and transparently, and only where one of the six legal bases in Article 6(1) applies. A basis in a legal obligation or a public task has to be laid down by Union law or by Member State law to which the controller is subject. The legal basis is part of the information due under Articles 13 and 14, which are a separate row.
rows.note: The published mapping lists the clauses titled "Identify lawful basis" (7.2.2) and "Organization’s purposes" (8.2.2). The Privacy Framework asks for processing to be authorised, with consent as one example; it sets out no list of legal bases. Which basis fits a purpose is a question of Article 6, not of the Framework. Transparency is worked out in the rows on Articles 12 to 14.

gdpr.label: Article 5(1)(b)
gdpr.title: Principles relating to processing of personal data

gdpr.label: Article 6(4)
gdpr.title: Lawfulness of processing

rows.obligation: Collect personal data for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and do not process them further in a way that is incompatible with those purposes. Further processing for archiving in the public interest, scientific or historical research or statistics in accordance with Article 89(1) is not considered incompatible. Where a new purpose rests neither on consent nor on a Union or Member State law that is a necessary and proportionate measure to safeguard an objective listed in Article 23(1), assess compatibility taking into account, among other things, the factors in Article 6(4): the link between the purposes, the context of collection, the nature of the data, the possible consequences for individuals and the existence of appropriate safeguards.
rows.note: The published mapping lists among others the clauses titled "Identify and document purpose" (7.2.1) and "Organization’s purposes" (8.2.2). The Privacy Framework asks for purposes to be inventoried; it does not set out the compatibility test of Article 6(4), so a recorded purpose shows what the purpose was, not that a new use is compatible with it.

gdpr.label: Article 5(1)(c) and (e)
gdpr.title: Principles relating to processing of personal data

rows.obligation: Keep personal data adequate, relevant and limited to what the purposes need, and keep them in a form that permits identification for no longer than those purposes require. Longer storage is allowed only for archiving in the public interest, research or statistics, with the safeguards of Article 89(1).
rows.note: The published mapping lists the clauses titled "Limit collection", "PII minimization objectives", "PII de-identification and deletion at the end of processing" and "Temporary files". The Privacy Framework addresses minimisation and storage limitation through disassociated processing and destruction according to policy. The retention period itself comes from the purpose and from sector law.

gdpr.label: Article 5(1)(d)
gdpr.title: Principles relating to processing of personal data

rows.obligation: Keep personal data accurate and, where necessary, up to date. Take every reasonable step to erase or rectify without delay data that are inaccurate for the purposes they are processed for.
rows.note: Accuracy as a principle applies whether or not anyone asks for a correction; the right to rectification is a separate row.

gdpr.label: Article 7
gdpr.title: Conditions for consent

gdpr.label: Article 8
gdpr.title: Conditions applicable to child's consent in relation to information society services

rows.obligation: Where processing relies on consent, be able to demonstrate it. Where consent is given in a written declaration that also concerns other matters, present the request for consent so that it is clearly distinguishable from them, in an intelligible and easily accessible form and in clear and plain language. Tell individuals before they consent that they can withdraw at any time, and make withdrawal as easy as giving consent. When judging whether consent is freely given, take utmost account of whether the performance of a contract, including the provision of a service, is made conditional on consent to processing that the contract does not need. Where consent is the basis for an information society service offered directly to a child who is below the age of 16, or below the lower age a Member State sets, which may not be under 13, the consent has to be given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility, and the controller makes reasonable efforts to verify this, taking into consideration available technology.
rows.note: The Privacy Framework covers obtaining, maintaining and revoking authorisations. It has no outcome on children's consent, on verifying parental authorisation or on consent bundled with a contract.

gdpr.label: Article 9
gdpr.title: Processing of special categories of personal data

gdpr.label: Article 10
gdpr.title: Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences

rows.obligation: Do not process special categories of personal data unless one of the conditions in Article 9(2) applies, in addition to a legal basis under Article 6. Process data on criminal convictions and offences only under the control of official authority or where Union or Member State law authorises it with appropriate safeguards.
rows.note: The published mapping lists only the clauses titled "Identify lawful basis" (7.2.2) and "Obtain and record consent" (7.2.4). The Privacy Framework treats data sensitivity as a contextual factor in risk assessment; it defines no special categories and no conditions for processing them. Recital 51 says that the conditions for lawful processing apply in addition to the specific requirements for special categories.

gdpr.label: Article 5(2)
gdpr.title: Principles relating to processing of personal data

gdpr.label: Article 24
gdpr.title: Responsibility of the controller

rows.obligation: Be responsible for compliance with the principles and be able to demonstrate it. Implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, taking into account the nature, scope, context, purposes and risks of the processing, to ensure and to be able to demonstrate that processing complies with the Regulation; review and update them where necessary, and adopt data protection policies where that is proportionate.
rows.note: This is the obligation closest to what a management framework is for. Records produced under the Privacy Framework can support a demonstration of accountability under Article 5(2); they do not replace the measures each of the other rows requires. The published mapping lists among others the clauses titled "Policies for information security" (6.2.1.1) and "Records related to processing PII" (7.2.8).

gdpr.label: Article 12
gdpr.title: Transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of the rights of the data subject

gdpr.label: Article 11
gdpr.title: Processing which does not require identification

rows.obligation: Give information and communications to individuals in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, in clear and plain language, and make it easy for them to exercise their rights. Tell the individual what was done about a request without undue delay and within one month of receiving it; the period can be extended by two further months where the complexity and number of requests make that necessary, and the individual has to be told of the extension and its reasons within the first month. If no action is taken, say why within one month and point to the right to complain and to go to court. Requests are handled free of charge unless manifestly unfounded or excessive, which the controller has to show; then a reasonable fee or a refusal is allowed. Where there are reasonable doubts about identity, the controller may ask for the information needed to confirm it. Where the purposes do not require identifying individuals and the controller can show that it cannot identify the person, it says so if possible, and Articles 15 to 20 do not apply unless the individual supplies information that enables identification.
rows.note: The Privacy Framework asks for policies and mechanisms for requests and communication. It sets no time limit, no rule on fees and no standard of plain language; those come from Article 12.

gdpr.label: Article 13
gdpr.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject

gdpr.label: Article 14
gdpr.title: Information to be provided where personal data have not been obtained from the data subject

rows.obligation: Tell individuals who the controller is and how to reach it and the data protection officer, the purposes and legal basis, the legitimate interests relied on, the recipients, any transfers and their safeguards, the retention period, their rights including withdrawal of consent, the right to complain, and whether automated decision-making takes place, with meaningful information about its logic and consequences. Do this at collection when the data come from the individual; otherwise within a reasonable period and at most one month, and no later than the first communication with the individual or the first disclosure to another recipient. Say whether providing the data is required when collecting directly, and name the source and the categories of data when collecting from elsewhere. Inform individuals again before processing for a new purpose. No information is due where the individual already has it; Article 14(5) lists further exceptions for data obtained from elsewhere.
rows.note: The published mapping lists the clauses titled "Determining information for PII principals" and "Providing information to PII principals" among others. The Privacy Framework asks for notices and transparency policies on purposes, practices and risks; the detailed list of items is in Articles 13 and 14.

gdpr.label: Article 15
gdpr.title: Right of access by the data subject

rows.obligation: Confirm on request whether personal data are being processed and give access to them, with the purposes, the categories of data, the recipients, the retention period, the source, the individual's rights and information on automated decision-making and on transfer safeguards. Provide a copy of the data, the first one free of charge and further copies for a reasonable fee at most, in a commonly used electronic form when the request is made electronically unless the individual asks otherwise, without adversely affecting the rights and freedoms of others.
rows.note: The published mapping lists among others the clauses titled "Providing copy of PII processed" (7.3.8) and "Handling requests" (7.3.9). The Privacy Framework supports the mechanics: finding the data, the recipients and the source. The list of information to give with the copy comes from Article 15(1) and (2), and the time limit is in the row on Article 12.

gdpr.label: Article 16
gdpr.title: Right to rectification

gdpr.label: Article 19
gdpr.title: Notification obligation regarding rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing

rows.obligation: Rectify inaccurate personal data and complete incomplete data without undue delay when the individual asks. Tell each recipient the data were disclosed to, unless that is impossible or involves disproportionate effort, and tell the individual who those recipients are on request.

gdpr.label: Article 17
gdpr.title: Right to erasure (‘right to be forgotten’)

gdpr.label: Article 19
gdpr.title: Notification obligation regarding rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing

rows.obligation: Erase personal data without undue delay where a ground in Article 17(1) applies, for example the data are no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn and no other legal ground remains, an objection succeeds or the data were processed unlawfully. Article 17(1) states this both as a right of the individual and as an obligation of the controller. The duty does not apply to the extent that an exception in Article 17(3) applies. Where the controller has made the data public, take reasonable steps, taking account of available technology and cost, to inform other controllers processing them that the individual has requested erasure of links and copies. Notify recipients under Article 19 and tell the individual who those recipients are on request.
rows.note: The published mapping lists among others the clauses titled "Access, correction and/or erasure" (7.3.6) and "PII controllers' obligations to inform third parties" (7.3.7). The Privacy Framework gives the ability to delete and to pass the deletion on. Whether a ground or an exception applies is a legal assessment each time.

gdpr.label: Article 18
gdpr.title: Right to restriction of processing

gdpr.label: Article 19
gdpr.title: Notification obligation regarding rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing

rows.obligation: Restrict processing on request while accuracy or an objection is being verified, where the processing is unlawful and the individual prefers restriction to erasure, or where the controller no longer needs the data but the individual needs them for legal claims. Restricted data may be stored but otherwise processed only with consent or on the limited grounds in Article 18(2). Tell the individual before the restriction is lifted, notify recipients under Article 19 and tell the individual who those recipients are on request.
rows.note: No subcategory describes restriction as a state of the data. The nearest is carrying processing permissions with the data elements, which is one way to implement it. The subcategory on passing corrections and deletions on to recipients (CM.AW-P5) does not mention restrictions, so notifying the recipients under Article 19 has no counterpart here; the record of disclosures supports telling the individual who the recipients are.

gdpr.label: Article 20
gdpr.title: Right to data portability

rows.obligation: Where processing is automated and rests on consent or on a contract, give individuals the personal data they provided in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format, and transmit the data directly to another controller where that is technically feasible. The right must not adversely affect the rights and freedoms of others.
rows.note: The published mapping lists one clause, titled "Providing copy of PII processed" (7.3.8).

gdpr.label: Article 21
gdpr.title: Right to object

rows.obligation: Stop processing that is based on a public task or on legitimate interests when the individual objects on grounds relating to their particular situation, unless the controller demonstrates compelling legitimate grounds that override the individual's interests, rights and freedoms, or the data are needed for legal claims. Stop direct marketing, and profiling for it, whenever the individual objects. Bring the right to the individual's attention explicitly and separately from other information, at the latest at the first communication.
rows.note: The published mapping lists among others the clause titled "Provide mechanism to object to PII processing" (7.3.5). The Privacy Framework handles the request and the notice; the weighing of compelling grounds against the individual's interests is a legal test with no counterpart in it, and it has no outcome on presenting the right separately from other information.

gdpr.label: Article 22
gdpr.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling

rows.obligation: Do not subject individuals to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects or similarly significant effects on them, unless it is necessary for a contract, authorised by law with safeguards, or based on explicit consent. In the contract and consent cases, provide at least human intervention and the means to express a view and to contest the decision. Such decisions may rest on special categories of data only under Article 9(2)(a) or (g), with suitable measures.
rows.note: The published mapping lists the clauses titled "Identify lawful basis" (7.2.2) and "Automated decision making" (7.3.10). The Privacy Framework has an outcome on evaluating analytic inputs and outputs for bias (ID.RA-P2). It is not cited, because Article 22 does not name such a measure. The Framework has no outcome on human intervention, on expressing a point of view or on contesting a decision.

gdpr.label: Article 25
gdpr.title: Data protection by design and by default

rows.obligation: Build data protection into processing from the design stage and throughout, with measures such as pseudonymisation that implement the principles and integrate the necessary safeguards, taking account of the state of the art, the cost, the nature of the processing and the risks. By default, process only the personal data necessary for each purpose, in amount, extent of processing, storage period and accessibility, so that data are not made accessible to an indefinite number of people without the individual's intervention.

gdpr.label: Article 30
gdpr.title: Records of processing activities

rows.obligation: Controllers keep a written record of processing activities with the name and contact details of the controller and, where applicable, of the joint controller, the representative and the data protection officer, the purposes, the categories of individuals, data and recipients, transfers and, where possible, retention periods and a general description of the security measures; processors keep a record of the categories of processing carried out for each controller. Make the record available to the supervisory authority on request. An organisation with fewer than 250 employees is exempt only if its processing is occasional, is not likely to result in a risk and includes no special category or criminal conviction data.
rows.note: The inventory subcategories of the Privacy Framework ask for more detail than Article 30 in some respects, for example data actions and data elements per system, and for less in others: none asks for erasure time limits, contact details or a description of security measures in the inventory. The Privacy Framework also has no outcome on making the record available to a supervisory authority. A Commission proposal to amend the exemption in Article 30(5), COM(2025) 501, was still in procedure on 16 November 2026; the row states the law in force.

gdpr.label: Article 35
gdpr.title: Data protection impact assessment

rows.obligation: Before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, in particular with new technologies, assess its impact: describe the processing and its purposes, assess necessity and proportionality, assess the risks to individuals and set out the measures that address them. The assessment is required in particular in the three cases of Article 35(3) and for processing on the supervisory authority's list. Seek the advice of the data protection officer, where one is designated, and, where appropriate, the views of individuals. Where necessary, and at least when the risk changes, review whether the processing still matches the assessment.
rows.note: The published mapping lists among others the clause titled "Privacy impact assessment" (7.2.5). The Privacy Framework runs risk assessment as a standing activity for all processing; Article 35 adds a trigger and required contents, and Article 36 ties the result to prior consultation.

gdpr.label: Article 36
gdpr.title: Prior consultation

rows.obligation: Consult the supervisory authority before processing where the impact assessment indicates that the processing would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate it. Give the authority the information listed in Article 36(3), including the assessment and the contact details of the data protection officer. Where the authority considers that the processing would infringe the GDPR, it gives written advice within eight weeks, extendable by six.
rows.note: The Privacy Framework has no outcome about consulting a regulator before processing starts. The NIST-hosted GDPR crosswalk pairs this article with four inventory subcategories and with the one on feedback from individuals; this site reads none of them as addressing the duty to consult.

gdpr.label: Article 37
gdpr.title: Designation of the data protection officer

gdpr.label: Article 38
gdpr.title: Position of the data protection officer

gdpr.label: Article 39
gdpr.title: Tasks of the data protection officer

rows.obligation: Designate a data protection officer where a public authority or body carries out the processing (courts acting in their judicial capacity excepted), where core activities consist of regular and systematic monitoring of individuals on a large scale or of large-scale processing of special category or criminal conviction data, or where Union or Member State law requires it. Choose the officer for professional qualities, in particular expert knowledge of data protection law and practice, publish the contact details and give them to the supervisory authority, involve the officer properly and in good time in all data protection matters, and provide resources. Give no instructions on the tasks, do not dismiss or penalise the officer for performing them, have the officer report to the highest management level, and make sure other duties cause no conflict of interests. The officer's tasks are at least to inform and advise, to monitor compliance, to advise on impact assessments, and to cooperate with the supervisory authority and act as its contact point.
rows.note: The published mapping lists three clauses, all under clause 6, which the mapping project labels "Guidance related to ISO/IEC 27002": "Information security roles and responsibilities", "Information security awareness, education and training" and "Confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements". The Privacy Framework asks for privacy roles and responsibilities to be established for the workforce; it says nothing on independence, protection from dismissal or the reporting line.

gdpr.label: Article 27
gdpr.title: Representatives of controllers or processors not established in the Union

rows.obligation: A controller or processor that is not established in the Union but is subject to the GDPR under Article 3(2) designates in writing a representative in a Member State where the individuals concerned are. No representative is needed where the processing is occasional, includes no large-scale special category or criminal conviction data and is unlikely to result in a risk, or for a public authority or body. Supervisory authorities and individuals can address the representative in addition to or instead of the organisation.
rows.note: The published mapping lists one clause, "Information security roles and responsibilities" (6.3.1.1). The Privacy Framework has no outcome about a representative in another jurisdiction. The NIST-hosted GDPR crosswalk pairs this article with six subcategories on workforce and communication roles, training and policy review; this site reads none of them as addressing the designation of a representative.

gdpr.label: Article 31
gdpr.title: Cooperation with the supervisory authority

rows.obligation: Cooperate with the supervisory authority, on request, in the performance of its tasks. The duty applies to controllers, processors and their representatives.
rows.note: The published mapping lists the clause titled "Understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties" (5.2.2). The Privacy Framework has no outcome about dealing with a regulator. The NIST-hosted GDPR crosswalk pairs this article with one subcategory, on feedback from individuals; this site does not read it as addressing cooperation with a supervisory authority.

gdpr.label: Article 26
gdpr.title: Joint controllers

rows.obligation: Where two or more controllers jointly determine the purposes and means of processing, set out in a transparent arrangement who does what, in particular for the rights of individuals and the information duties, unless the law already allocates the responsibilities. Make the essence of the arrangement available to individuals, who can exercise their rights against each of the controllers.
rows.note: The published mapping lists the clause titled "Joint PII controller" (7.2.7). The Privacy Framework has roles identified and aligned with third parties, by contract where needed; it has no outcome on making the arrangement available to individuals.

gdpr.label: Article 28(1)
gdpr.title: Processor

rows.obligation: Use only processors that provide sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, so that the processing meets the requirements of the GDPR and protects the rights of individuals.
rows.note: The published mapping lists two clauses under clause 6, which the mapping project labels "Guidance related to ISO/IEC 27002": "Addressing security within supplier agreements" (6.12.1.2) and "Identification of applicable legislation and contractual requirements" (6.15.1.1).

gdpr.label: Article 28(3) and (9)
gdpr.title: Processor

rows.obligation: Govern processing by a processor through a contract or other legal act, in writing including in electronic form, that binds the processor and sets out the subject matter and duration of the processing, its nature and purpose, the type of personal data, the categories of individuals and the obligations and rights of the controller. The contract has to contain the terms in Article 28(3)(a) to (h).
rows.note: The published mapping lists the clauses titled "Contracts with PII processors" (7.2.6) and "Customer agreement" (8.2.1) against Article 28(9); the clauses it lists for the individual terms of Article 28(3) are on the rows for those terms, including the security row. The Privacy Framework asks for contracts that implement the privacy programme; the list of required terms is in Article 28(3).

gdpr.label: Article 28(2), (3)(d) and (4)
gdpr.title: Processor

rows.obligation: A processor engages another processor only with the controller's prior specific or general written authorisation and, under a general authorisation, informs the controller of intended changes so that the controller can object. It imposes the same data protection obligations on the other processor by contract and stays fully liable to the controller for that processor's performance.
rows.note: The published mapping lists among others the clauses titled "Disclosure of subcontractors used to process PII", "Engagement of a subcontractor to process PII" and "Change of subcontractor to process PII" (8.5.6 to 8.5.8). The Privacy Framework has third parties identified, assessed and bound by contract; it has no outcome on asking the customer before engaging one.

gdpr.label: Article 28(3)(a)
gdpr.title: Processor

gdpr.label: Article 29
gdpr.title: Processing under the authority of the controller or processor

gdpr.label: Article 32(4)
gdpr.title: Security of processing

rows.obligation: A processor processes personal data only on documented instructions from the controller, including for transfers to a third country or an international organisation, unless Union or Member State law to which it is subject requires the processing; in that case it informs the controller of the legal requirement before processing, unless that law prohibits the information on important grounds of public interest. Controller and processor each take steps to ensure that anyone acting under their authority who has access to personal data processes them only on instructions from the controller, unless Union or Member State law requires otherwise.
rows.note: The Privacy Framework covers authorising processing and the workforce knowing its role. It has no outcome on processing only on the instructions of the organisation the data are processed for.

gdpr.label: Article 28(3)(e) to (h)
gdpr.title: Processor

rows.obligation: Under the terms that Article 28(3)(e) to (h) requires in the contract, the processor assists the controller, as far as possible, with requests from individuals, and with security, breach notification, impact assessments and prior consultation. After the end of the service it deletes or returns all personal data, at the controller's choice, and deletes existing copies unless Union or Member State law requires storage. It makes available the information needed to demonstrate compliance with Article 28 and allows for and contributes to audits and inspections. It tells the controller immediately if it considers that an instruction infringes the GDPR or other Union or Member State data protection provisions.
rows.note: The published mapping lists among others the clauses titled "Obligations to PII principals" (8.3.1), "Return, transfer or disposal of PII" (8.4.2) and "Infringing instruction" (8.2.4). The Privacy Framework has no outcome on flagging an unlawful instruction. Its outcomes on auditing third parties are written for the organisation that instructs, and are cited on the row on choosing processors; it has none on submitting to an audit.

gdpr.label: Article 32(1) and (2)
gdpr.title: Security of processing

gdpr.label: Article 5(1)(f)
gdpr.title: Principles relating to processing of personal data

gdpr.label: Article 28(3)(b) and (c)
gdpr.title: Processor

rows.obligation: Implement technical and organisational measures that give a level of security appropriate to the risk, including as appropriate pseudonymisation and encryption, the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems, the ability to restore access to data in good time after an incident, and regular testing and evaluation of the measures. In assessing the appropriate level of security, take account in particular of the risks of accidental or unlawful destruction, loss or alteration of the data and of unauthorised disclosure of or access to them. The contract with a processor has to require that the people authorised to process the data are bound to confidentiality, by commitment or by statute, and that the processor takes the measures Article 32 requires.
rows.note: This is the row with the most references on both sides: the published mapping lists more clauses for the provisions of this row than for any other row, most of them under clause 6, which the mapping project labels "Guidance related to ISO/IEC 27002", and all 30 subcategories of Protect-P bear on it. The row cites the subcategories nearest to the measures the article names. What is appropriate to the risk in a given case is for the controller or processor to assess under Article 32(1) and (2); the Privacy Framework does not decide it.

gdpr.label: Article 33(1) and (3) to (5)
gdpr.title: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority

rows.obligation: Notify the competent supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals; give reasons for any delay. Describe the breach, its likely consequences and the measures taken, give a contact point, and document every breach, its effects and the remedial action so that the authority can verify compliance.
rows.note: The published mapping lists the clauses titled "Responsibilities and procedures" (6.13.1.1) and "Response to information security incidents" (6.13.1.5). The Privacy Framework has response plans established and managed. Its notification outcome (CM.AW-P7) names impacted individuals and organisations, which this site reads as not covering the supervisory authority; the 72 hours, the risk threshold and the breach register come from Article 33. The Digital Omnibus proposal, COM(2025) 837, would amend Article 33; it was still in procedure on 16 November 2026 and the row states the law in force.

gdpr.label: Article 33(2)
gdpr.title: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority

rows.obligation: The processor notifies the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach.
rows.note: The duty has no risk threshold: the processor reports every personal data breach and the controller assesses it. The Privacy Framework sets no time for the notification.

gdpr.label: Article 34
gdpr.title: Communication of a personal data breach to the data subject

rows.obligation: Where a breach is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, tell them without undue delay, in clear and plain language, what happened, the likely consequences, the measures taken and whom to contact. No communication is needed where appropriate protection measures had been applied to the data, in particular measures that make them unintelligible to unauthorised persons, such as encryption, or where later measures mean the high risk is no longer likely to materialise; where it would take disproportionate effort, a public communication is made instead. The supervisory authority can require the communication.
rows.note: The Privacy Framework has affected individuals notified and response plans in place; the high-risk threshold, the content of the communication and the exemptions come from Article 34.

gdpr.label: Article 44
gdpr.title: General principle for transfers

gdpr.label: Article 45
gdpr.title: Transfers on the basis of an adequacy decision

gdpr.label: Article 46
gdpr.title: Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards

gdpr.label: Article 47
gdpr.title: Binding corporate rules

rows.obligation: Transfer personal data to a third country or an international organisation only if the conditions of Chapter V are met, so that the level of protection is not undermined, including for onward transfers. That means an adequacy decision or, failing that, appropriate safeguards such as standard data protection clauses, approved binding corporate rules, or an approved code of conduct or certification with binding commitments, on condition that enforceable rights and effective legal remedies are available to individuals. Failing both, only the derogations of Article 49 remain, which are a separate row.
rows.note: The published mapping lists two clauses, "Identify basis for PII transfer between jurisdictions" (7.5.1, for controllers) and "Basis for PII transfer between jurisdictions" (8.5.1, for processors). The Privacy Framework governs disclosure by policy and third parties by contract; it has no outcome on the conditions for sending data abroad. The derogations of Article 49 are a separate row.

gdpr.label: Article 49
gdpr.title: Derogations for specific situations

rows.obligation: Without an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards, transfer only under a derogation in Article 49(1), such as explicit consent after being informed of the risks, necessity for a contract with or in the interest of the individual, important reasons of public interest, or legal claims. The last-resort ground of compelling legitimate interests that the individual's interests and rights do not override covers only a transfer that is not repetitive and concerns a limited number of individuals, after an assessment and with suitable safeguards; the controller informs the supervisory authority and the individuals, and the controller or processor documents the assessment and the safeguards in the Article 30 record.
rows.note: The published mapping lists the same two clauses as for Articles 44 to 47, "Identify basis for PII transfer between jurisdictions" (7.5.1) and "Basis for PII transfer between jurisdictions" (8.5.1). The Privacy Framework has no counterpart to the derogations; the two references show only where a decision to transfer is authorised and governed by procedure.

gdpr.label: Article 48
gdpr.title: Transfers or disclosures not authorised by Union law

rows.obligation: A judgment of a court or a decision of an administrative authority of a third country that requires a controller or processor to transfer or disclose personal data is recognised or enforceable only if it is based on an international agreement, such as a mutual legal assistance treaty, in force between that country and the Union or a Member State. The other grounds for transfer in Chapter V are not affected.
rows.note: The published mapping adds the clause titled "Legally binding PII disclosures" (8.5.5) to the two transfer clauses. The Privacy Framework has disclosures governed by policy; the test for a foreign demand is in Article 48.

nist.name: IDENTIFY-P
nist.text: Develop the organizational understanding to manage privacy risk for individuals arising from data processing.

cats.name: Inventory and Mapping
cats.text: Data processing by systems, products, or services is understood and informs the management of privacy risk.

subs.text: Systems/products/services that process data are inventoried.

Owners or operators (e.g., the organization or third parties such as service providers, partners, customers, and developers) and their roles with respect to the systems/products/services and components (e.g., internal or external) that process data are inventoried.
Categories of individuals (e.g., customers, employees or prospective employees, consumers) whose data are being processed are inventoried.
Data actions of the systems/products/services are inventoried.
The purposes for the data actions are inventoried.
Data elements within the data actions are inventoried.
The data processing environment is identified (e.g., geographic location, internal, cloud, third parties).

Data processing is mapped, illustrating the data actions and associated data elements for systems/products/services, including components; roles of the component owners/operators; and interactions of individuals or third parties with the systems/products/services.

cats.name: Business Environment
cats.text: The organization’s mission, objectives, stakeholders, and activities are understood and prioritized; this information is used to inform privacy roles, responsibilities, and risk management decisions.

subs.text: The organization’s role(s) in the data processing ecosystem are identified and communicated.
Priorities for organizational mission, objectives, and activities are established and communicated.
Systems/products/services that support organizational priorities are identified and key requirements communicated.

cats.name: Risk Assessment
cats.text: The organization understands the privacy risks to individuals and how such privacy risks may create follow-on impacts on organizational operations, including mission, functions, other risk management priorities (e.g., compliance, financial), reputation, workforce, and culture.

subs.text: Contextual factors related to the systems/products/services and the data actions are identified (e.g., individuals’ demographics and privacy interests or perceptions, data sensitivity and/or types, visibility of data processing to individuals and third parties).
Data analytic inputs and outputs are identified and evaluated for bias.
Potential problematic data actions and associated problems are identified.
Problematic data actions, likelihoods, and impacts are used to determine and prioritize risk.
Risk responses are identified, prioritized, and implemented.

cats.name: Data Processing Ecosystem Risk Management
cats.text: The organization’s priorities, constraints, risk tolerance, and assumptions are established and used to support risk decisions associated with managing privacy risk and third parties within the data processing ecosystem. The organization has established and implemented the processes to identify, assess, and manage privacy risks within the data processing ecosystem.

subs.text: Data processing ecosystem risk management policies, processes, and procedures are identified, established, assessed, managed, and agreed to by organizational stakeholders.

Data processing ecosystem parties (e.g., service providers, customers, partners, product manufacturers, application developers) are identified, prioritized, and assessed using a privacy risk assessment process.
Contracts with data processing ecosystem parties are used to implement appropriate measures designed to meet the objectives of an organization’s privacy program.
Interoperability frameworks or similar multi-party approaches are used to manage data processing ecosystem privacy risks.

Data processing ecosystem parties are routinely assessed using audits, test results, or other forms of evaluations to confirm they are meeting their contractual, interoperability framework, or other obligations.

nist.name: GOVERN-P
nist.text: Develop and implement the organizational governance structure to enable an ongoing understanding of the organization’s risk management priorities that are informed by privacy risk.

cats.name: Governance Policies, Processes, and Procedures
cats.text: The policies, processes, and procedures to manage and monitor the organization’s regulatory, legal, risk, environmental, and operational requirements are understood and inform the management of privacy risk.

subs.text: Organizational privacy values and policies (e.g., conditions on data processing such as data uses or retention periods, individuals’ prerogatives with respect to data processing) are established and communicated.
Processes to instill organizational privacy values within system/product/service development and operations are established and in place.
Roles and responsibilities for the workforce are established with respect to privacy.
Privacy roles and responsibilities are coordinated and aligned with third-party stakeholders (e.g., service providers, customers, partners).
Legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements regarding privacy are understood and managed.
Governance and risk management policies, processes, and procedures address privacy risks.

cats.name: Risk Management Strategy
cats.text: The organization’s priorities, constraints, risk tolerances, and assumptions are established and used to support operational risk decisions.

subs.text: Risk management processes are established, managed, and agreed to by organizational stakeholders.
Organizational risk tolerance is determined and clearly expressed.
The organization’s determination of risk tolerance is informed by its role(s) in the data processing ecosystem.

cats.name: Awareness and Training
cats.text: The organization’s workforce and third parties engaged in data processing are provided privacy awareness education and are trained to perform their privacy-related duties and responsibilities consistent with related policies, processes, procedures, and agreements and organizational privacy values.

subs.text: The workforce is informed and trained on its roles and responsibilities.
Senior executives understand their roles and responsibilities.
Privacy personnel understand their roles and responsibilities.
Third parties (e.g., service providers, customers, partners) understand their roles and responsibilities.

cats.name: Monitoring and Review
cats.text: The policies, processes, and procedures for ongoing review of the organization’s privacy posture are understood and inform the management of privacy risk.

subs.text: Privacy risk is re-evaluated on an ongoing basis and as key factors, including the organization’s business environment (e.g., introduction of new technologies), governance (e.g., legal obligations, risk tolerance), data processing, and systems/products/services change.
Privacy values, policies, and training are reviewed and any updates are communicated.
Policies, processes, and procedures for assessing compliance with legal requirements and privacy policies are established and in place.
Policies, processes, and procedures for communicating progress on managing privacy risks are established and in place.

Policies, processes, and procedures are established and in place to receive, analyze, and respond to problematic data actions disclosed to the organization from internal and external sources (e.g., internal discovery, privacy researchers, professional events).
Policies, processes, and procedures incorporate lessons learned from problematic data actions.

Policies, processes, and procedures for receiving, tracking, and responding to complaints, concerns, and questions from individuals about organizational privacy practices are established and in place.

nist.name: CONTROL-P
nist.text: Develop and implement appropriate activities to enable organizations or individuals to manage data with sufficient granularity to manage privacy risks.

cats.name: Data Processing Policies, Processes, and Procedures
cats.text: Policies, processes, and procedures are maintained and used to manage data processing (e.g., purpose, scope, roles and responsibilities in the data processing ecosystem, and management commitment) consistent with the organization’s risk strategy to protect individuals’ privacy.

subs.text: Policies, processes, and procedures for authorizing data processing (e.g., organizational decisions, individual consent), revoking authorizations, and maintaining authorizations are established and in place.

Policies, processes, and procedures for enabling data review, transfer, sharing or disclosure, alteration, and deletion are established and in place (e.g., to maintain data quality, manage data retention).
Policies, processes, and procedures for enabling individuals’ data processing preferences and requests are established and in place.
A data life cycle to manage data is aligned and implemented with the system development life cycle to manage systems.

cats.name: Data Processing Management
cats.text: Data are managed consistent with the organization’s risk strategy to protect individuals’ privacy, increase manageability, and enable the implementation of privacy principles (e.g., individual participation, data quality, data minimization).

subs.text: Data elements can be accessed for review.
Data elements can be accessed for transmission or disclosure.
Data elements can be accessed for alteration.
Data elements can be accessed for deletion.
Data are destroyed according to policy.
Data are transmitted using standardized formats.
Mechanisms for transmitting processing permissions and related data values with data elements are established and in place.
Audit/log records are determined, documented, implemented, and reviewed in accordance with policy and incorporating the principle of data minimization.
Technical measures implemented to manage data processing are tested and assessed.
Stakeholder privacy preferences are included in algorithmic design objectives and outputs are evaluated against these preferences.

cats.name: Disassociated Processing
cats.text: Data processing solutions increase disassociability consistent with the organization’s risk strategy to protect individuals’ privacy and enable implementation of privacy principles (e.g., data minimization).

subs.text: Data are processed to limit observability and linkability (e.g., data actions take place on local devices, privacy-preserving cryptography).
Data are processed to limit the identification of individuals (e.g., de-identification privacy techniques, tokenization).
Data are processed to limit the formulation of inferences about individuals’ behavior or activities (e.g., data processing is decentralized, distributed architectures).
System or device configurations permit selective collection or disclosure of data elements.
Attribute references are substituted for attribute values.

nist.name: COMMUNICATE-P
nist.text: Develop and implement appropriate activities to enable organizations and individuals to have a reliable understanding and engage in a dialogue about how data are processed and associated privacy risks.

cats.name: Communication Policies, Processes, and Procedures
cats.text: Policies, processes, and procedures are maintained and used to increase transparency of the organization’s data processing practices (e.g., purpose, scope, roles and responsibilities in the data processing ecosystem, and management commitment) and associated privacy risks.

subs.text: Transparency policies, processes, and procedures for communicating data processing purposes, practices, and associated privacy risks are established and in place.
Roles and responsibilities (e.g., public relations) for communicating data processing purposes, practices, and associated privacy risks are established.

cats.name: Data Processing Awareness
cats.text: Individuals and organizations have reliable knowledge about data processing practices and associated privacy risks, and effective mechanisms are used and maintained to increase predictability consistent with the organization’s risk strategy to protect individuals’ privacy.

subs.text: Mechanisms (e.g., notices, internal or public reports) for communicating data processing purposes, practices, associated privacy risks, and options for enabling individuals’ data processing preferences and requests are established and in place.
Mechanisms for obtaining feedback from individuals (e.g., surveys or focus groups) about data processing and associated privacy risks are established and in place.
System/product/service design enables data processing visibility.
Records of data disclosures and sharing are maintained and can be accessed for review or transmission/disclosure.
Data corrections or deletions can be communicated to individuals or organizations (e.g., data sources) in the data processing ecosystem.
Data provenance and lineage are maintained and can be accessed for review or transmission/disclosure.
Impacted individuals and organizations are notified about a privacy breach or event.
Individuals are provided with mitigation mechanisms (e.g., credit monitoring, consent withdrawal, data alteration or deletion) to address impacts of problematic data actions.

nist.name: PROTECT-P
nist.text: Develop and implement appropriate data processing safeguards.

cats.name: Data Protection Policies, Processes, and Procedures
cats.text: Security and privacy policies (e.g., purpose, scope, roles and responsibilities in the data processing ecosystem, and management commitment), processes, and procedures are maintained and used to manage the protection of data.

subs.text: A baseline configuration of information technology is created and maintained incorporating security principles (e.g., concept of least functionality).
Configuration change control processes are established and in place.
Backups of information are conducted, maintained, and tested.
Policy and regulations regarding the physical operating environment for organizational assets are met.
Protection processes are improved.
Effectiveness of protection technologies is shared.
Response plans (Incident Response and Business Continuity) and recovery plans (Incident Recovery and Disaster Recovery) are established, in place, and managed.
Response and recovery plans are tested.
Privacy procedures are included in human resources practices (e.g., deprovisioning, personnel screening).
A vulnerability management plan is developed and implemented.

cats.name: Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control
cats.text: Access to data and devices is limited to authorized individuals, processes, and devices, and is managed consistent with the assessed risk of unauthorized access.

subs.text: Identities and credentials are issued, managed, verified, revoked, and audited for authorized individuals, processes, and devices.
Physical access to data and devices is managed.
Remote access is managed.
Access permissions and authorizations are managed, incorporating the principles of least privilege and separation of duties.
Network integrity is protected (e.g., network segregation, network segmentation).

Individuals and devices are proofed and bound to credentials, and authenticated commensurate with the risk of the transaction (e.g., individuals’ security and privacy risks and other organizational risks).

cats.name: Data Security
cats.text: Data are managed consistent with the organization’s risk strategy to protect individuals’ privacy and maintain data confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

subs.text: Data-at-rest are protected.
Data-in-transit are protected.
Systems/products/services and associated data are formally managed throughout removal, transfers, and disposition.
Adequate capacity to ensure availability is maintained.
Protections against data leaks are implemented.
Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity.
The development and testing environment(s) are separate from the production environment.
Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify hardware integrity.

cats.name: Maintenance
cats.text: System maintenance and repairs are performed consistent with policies, processes, and procedures.

subs.text: Maintenance and repair of organizational assets are performed and logged, with approved and controlled tools.
Remote maintenance of organizational assets is approved, logged, and performed in a manner that prevents unauthorized access.

cats.name: Protective Technology
cats.text: Technical security solutions are managed to ensure the security and resilience of systems/products/services and associated data, consistent with related policies, processes, procedures, and agreements.

subs.text: Removable media is protected and its use restricted according to policy.
The principle of least functionality is incorporated by configuring systems to provide only essential capabilities.
Communications and control networks are protected.
Mechanisms (e.g., failsafe, load balancing, hot swap) are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations.
